stops.name: Burgdorf, New Year 1836: 'Renewal of Life'
stops.campa: At the turn of the year the vision arrives whole, and Fröbel writes it down under a title that is itself a proclamation: the year 1836 demands a renewal of life. The renewal of a people, he sees, cannot be legislated or preached; it must be grown, and it begins in the nursing of earliest childhood: a new institution, neither school nor asylum, where the smallest children unfold through play as plants in a tended garden. The thing now exists entire in the spirit. Only the body, the town, and the name remain to be found.
stops.quote: Erneuung des Lebens erfordert das neue Jahr 1836. (The new year 1836 demands a renewal of life.)
stops.quote_source: Title of Fröbel's manuscript essay, Burgdorf, 1836

stops.name: Burgdorf, departure: the sick wife, the homeward road
stops.campa: Wilhelmine's health breaks in the sharp mountain air, and the physicians order her away from Switzerland. Fröbel resigns his post; Langethal and Ferdinand Fröbel keep Burgdorf, Middendorff turns home to Keilhau. Husband and wife travel to Berlin to settle her inheritance, and in the capital's nurseries and infant-schools Fröbel studies what exists for small children and finds it dead: minding without unfolding. The idea conceived at Burgdorf hardens on the journey into resolve. He returns to the Thuringian hills carrying the kindergarten like a child coming to term.

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Haus über dem Keller: the first institution for small children
stops.campa: In 1837, in the little town of Blankenburg an hour's walk over the hills from Keilhau, Fröbel rents an old powder-mill house called 'über dem Keller' and opens his Institution for the Fostering of the Activity Impulse of Childhood and Youth: the first house on earth built around the play of small children. Balls, blocks, songs, ring-games in the garden: the fifty-five-year-old man sits on the floor among three-year-olds, and those who watch understand nothing yet. The institution has everything except its true name, which is still walking toward him.
stops.quote: Play is the purest, most spiritual activity of man at this stage... It gives, therefore, joy, freedom, contentment, inner and outer rest, peace with the world.
stops.quote_source: The Education of Man (1826), tr. W. N. Hailmann, the doctrine enacted at Blankenburg

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Gifts, and the Sunday paper of the children
stops.campa: The crystallographer's revelation becomes a toy: the soft ball first, then sphere, cylinder and cube, then the divided blocks: the Spielgaben, play-Gifts, each one the eternal law of unfolding placed into a child's hands. Fröbel and his helpers make them, box them, and carry them like colporteurs of a new scripture; from 1838 his Sonntagsblatt spreads the play-theory under the motto that is his whole confession: Come, let us live for our children. Toy-merchants shrug; mothers begin, slowly, to understand. The Gifts go out from Blankenburg into the world's nurseries.
stops.quote: Kommt, lasst uns unsern Kindern leben!

stops.name: Dresden, carrying the Gifts to the cities
stops.campa: Fröbel takes the new education on the road: Dresden, Leipzig, Frankfurt, Göttingen, lecturing on play and the Gifts, folding paper before assemblies of skeptical schoolmen and attentive mothers. In Dresden he opens a play-circle and speaks before the court city's educators: the spectacle of an old man demonstrating ball-games as the foundation of national renewal draws mockery and discipleship in equal measure. Every city he leaves keeps a knot of converted women. He has discovered his true army, the one the Prussian ministry will one day fear: mothers.

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the death of Wilhelmine
stops.campa: On 13 May 1839 Wilhelmine dies, worn through by twenty-one years of shared poverty and shared faith: the war-councillor's daughter who chose the hillside, whose fortune fed the institute and whose quiet sense steadied its founder. Fröbel walks from her deathbed back to the little ones of Blankenburg; grief in him always converts to work for children. The household of the childless couple had been all children; now the widower gives himself wholly to the youngest, and the last barrier of private life falls away.

stops.name: The Steiger above Blankenburg, the NAME arrives
stops.campa: Spring 1840. Fröbel walks with Middendorff and Barop over the Steiger pass toward Blankenburg, tormented for weeks by the want of a name for his youngest-born institution. On the height, with the town at their feet, he suddenly stops as if fettered to the spot; his eyes take on a strange refulgent brilliancy; and he shouts to the mountains so that it echoes to the four winds. Kindergarten: garden of children. The word is not coined, it is received; the hills of Thuringia are its first witnesses, and the echo has not yet died.
stops.quote: Eureka! I have it! KINDERGARTEN shall be the name of the new Institution!
stops.quote_source: Johannes Barop's reminiscence (c. 1862), in Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel, tr. Michaelis & Moore

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg town hall, founding of the Universal German Kindergarten
stops.campa: On 28 June 1840, amid the four-hundredth jubilee of Gutenberg's press, Fröbel gathers the town in the Blankenburg Rathaus and founds the Allgemeiner Deutscher Kindergarten: deliberately yoking his institution to the printing press as the second great engine of the people's enlightenment. What Gutenberg did for the word, the kindergarten shall do for the child. Shares are subscribed, the women especially called to the work; the play-school 'über dem Keller' becomes the mother-garden of a planted world. From this hall the word Kindergarten begins its unstoppable emigration into every language on earth.

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Mutter- und Koselieder
stops.campa: In 1844 appears the strangest and tenderest of all pedagogical books: the Mutter- und Koselieder, mother-songs, caressing-songs, finger-plays, each with its picture, its melody, its whispered commentary to the mother. Pat-a-cake raised to philosophy: the weather-vane, the fish in the brook, the light-birds on the wall, every game a first lesson in the unity of life. It is the motherless man's letter to the mother he never had, dictated to every mother in Germany. Fröbel holds it the deepest of his books; the world will take a generation to agree.

stops.name: Rudolstadt, the teachers' assembly of the springtime of peoples
stops.campa: The revolutionary spring of 1848 raises every hope at once, and Fröbel's with them: now, surely, the new Germany will found itself upon the new childhood. At the great teachers' assembly in Rudolstadt in August, hundreds of schoolmen debate the people's education; Middendorff, Fröbel's Aaron, his spokesman since the bivouacs, pleads the kindergarten cause, and the assembly resolves that the kindergarten belongs in the free state's order. Petitions go to the Frankfurt parliament. For one bright year the garden of children and the garden of liberty seem to be one garden.

stops.name: Bad Liebenstein, 'the old fool' and the Baroness
stops.campa: Settled in a farmhouse by the spa of Liebenstein, Fröbel trains young women as kindergartners and dances ring-games in the meadow with the village children. The spa guests are told of 'the old fool' on the hill. In May 1849 the Baroness Bertha von Marenholtz-Bülow follows the phrase to its source, watches the grey-haired man leading his troop of children, and recognizes at sight what the villagers cannot: not a fool but a founder. She becomes the apostle of his cause to courts and salons: the interpreter the slow-tongued prophet has waited for all his life.

stops.name: Hamburg, the winter mission to the free city
stops.campa: Middendorff's eloquence has conquered Hamburg beforehand; in the winter of 1849–50 Fröbel comes in person, called by the women's association of the free city to lead courses for kindergartners at their new Hochschule for the female sex. The halting speaker after the golden-tongued herald disappoints the fashionable and wins the earnest: Wichard Lange, his future editor, attaches himself here. Hamburg's merchants' daughters learn finger-plays and the philosophy of play; the kindergarten takes root in the north. The women of Germany are becoming, parish by parish, the church of his idea.
